semantic_correction.stem: A nurse is caring for an adult client with an intellectual disability. A family member begins answering every question for the client. Which communication approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Address the client directly, use clear language, allow needed time, and rephrase or use another method if needed; involve the family without replacing the client.
options.B: Direct most questions to the family member and ask the client only for simple yes-or-no responses, because intellectual disability limits reliable participation.
options.C: Use the same communication style and pace used for every adult client, even when the client does not understand, because adapting the method can create dependence.
options.D: Ask the family member to interpret the client’s concerns before speaking with the client, then base explanations mainly on the family member’s understanding.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current CDC guidance for healthcare providers explicitly includes people with intellectual disabilities among patients for whom effective communication and accommodation may be needed. CDC instructs healthcare providers to communicate clearly and directly with the patient, repeat or rephrase questions or instructions or find another way to provide the information when the patient does not understand, and take the time needed to meet the patient’s healthcare needs. These principles support addressing the client rather than automatically redirecting the interaction to a family member. B is incorrect because an intellectual disability does not justify replacing direct patient communication with family-only communication or restricting the client to yes-or-no participation. C is incorrect because CDC specifically recommends adapting wording or the communication method when understanding is limited and allowing additional time when needed. D is incorrect because it makes the family member the default interpreter of the client’s concerns instead of first communicating directly with the client and individualizing assistance as needed.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Use respectful, individualized, direct communication with an adult who has an intellectual disability by addressing the client, adapting wording or communication methods when needed, allowing adequate time, and avoiding automatic substitution of family communication for the client’s own participation.

semantic_correction.source_locator: Overview, current web lines 49–53: healthcare professionals should know how to communicate effectively with patients who have a range of disabilities, including intellectual disability, and should plan for additional time when needed. What healthcare providers can do, lines 58–62: listen and respond to the patient’s health concerns; communicate clearly and directly with the patient; if the patient does not understand, repeat, use other words, or find another way to provide the information; take the time needed to meet the patient’s healthcare needs.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: CDC directly supports clear, direct communication with patients who have intellectual disabilities, adaptation of the communication method when needed, and adequate time rather than automatically replacing the patient’s participation with family communication.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests direct, respectful, individualized communication with an adult who has an intellectual disability, with one clearly best answer and no answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It directly applies CDC guidance to communicate clearly and directly with the patient, adapt wording or method when needed, and allow adequate time.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. It substitutes family communication for the patient and imposes an unsupported restriction to yes-or-no participation.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. CDC explicitly recommends rephrasing or using another method and allowing additional time rather than keeping a fixed communication style when the patient does not understand.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. It makes the family member the default source of the client’s meaning rather than addressing the patient directly first and individualizing assistance as needed.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone follows all current CDC communication principles; B and D replace direct patient participation with family communication, and C rejects the individualized adaptation CDC recommends.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel communication strategies with near-identical length and specificity; the prior uniquely-long correct option was removed and no conspicuous absolute-word cue identifies the key.
